message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) belong to the order **Carnivora** (family Felidae), while zebras (Equus quagga) belong to the order **Perissodactyla** (family Equidae).  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the two orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla – a member of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**.  

In other words, lions and zebras share a common ancestor that was a small, early Laurasiatherian mammal that lived roughly 55–60 million years ago during the late Paleocene/early Eocene. This ancestor gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually led to modern carnivores (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and odd-toed ungulates (horses, rhinos, tapirs, etc.).

Zebras are in order Perissodactyla, family Equidae. So their common ancestor would be at the level of mammals, maybe the last common ancestor of all placental mammals? But we can give a more specific answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be the common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria. So the common ancestor would be a mammal from the group Laurasiatheria, perhaps a small mammal from the Eocene. But the question might be simpler: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" The answer: They share a common ancestor at the level of mammals, specifically the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is part of Laurasiatheria. That ancestor lived around 55 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
